summary: Unpair a paired device from Settings, behind a confirmation that names the device and says the phone must pair again with a new PIN. First production caller of PairedClientRegistry.UnregisterClient, behind its own narrow IPairedDeviceRevoker. Clears FIVE stores - review found the file-transfer trust grant, which comes back as privilege rather than a label because that store prunes only for unpaired clients. Every teardown runs even when an earlier one throws (the original credential-first rationale was backwards: the registry is the first call and the only one that propagates), failures rethrown as AggregateException and reported by the command. Review PASS after two HIGHs fixed. Filed RemEx-6nkht (live session survives unpair) and RemEx-pynli (failed credential write brings the pairing back on restart). verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2098/2099; five injections all bit, one of which caught an inert guard of mine that asked the self-pruning trust API instead of the file on disk.

Unpairing a device now ends its live connections, not just future ones. IsClientPaired is consulted only when a connection is established, so a phone already mirroring the desktop kept mirroring it after being unpaired. Three channels, three owners: ClientSessionRegistry aborts every matching control socket (all of them, not Find's newest; IdentityProven-filtered so a loopback claimant cannot be used to cut the PC's own connection), DesktopSessionRegistry cancels the stream via its existing drain contract, TransferSessionManager aborts the file socket and lets RunChannelAsync's own finally suspend partials. PairedDeviceDisconnector hops off the caller's thread first, because otherwise the entire capture teardown unwound on the Avalonia dispatcher under a Settings button. Three review rounds, first two FAIL: round 1 found the UI-thread unwind, round 2 found that the fix for it had no guard (deleting the Task.Run left the suite green) plus two more inert guards and two throwing-logger escape routes, round 3 found CancelAsync had become load-bearing for the drain budget while its comment still called it a style choice. verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2113/2114; eight injections all bit.

A failed unpair now says whether the pairing will come back. UnregisterClient removes from memory then persists, so a failed write leaves the device unpaired for this run and untouched on disk - back on the next start. PairedDeviceRevocationException carries PairingMayReturn, set from whether the CREDENTIAL teardown failed rather than any failure, and the Settings command picks its wording from it. Review also caught that the new exception's Message is a constant where AggregateException's appended its inners, so the toast had silently lost the actual reason and was showing untranslated English in eight locales; Reason now joins the failures. Divergence test uses a per-OS injection (read-only file on Windows, write bit off the directory on Unix - rename consults the directory, not the target) and a probe that fails loudly under root rather than skipping. Three review rounds, first two FAIL: round 2 found the lost reason and that my guard had fabricated the Message it was testing; round 3 found every remaining assertion was direction-blind and would ship a swapped ternary green. verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2116/2117; five injections all bit.

The fifteenth was found earlier in the same diff by injection. Fixes not re-reviewed. Settled a question bead open since 2026-08-01 by taking the route it specified - tracing the compositor - rather than by reasoning from convention, which the bead explicitly warned against. mutter's discrete_steps_to_scroll_direction maps axis 0 steps>0 to CLUTTER_SCROLL_DOWN; KDE forwards steps unchanged to wl_pointer. The wire is Windows' positive-is-up. So the portal branch had scrolled backwards on every Wayland desktop since it was written, while both shell backends were always correct. HORIZONTAL IS NOT INVERTED - mutter maps axis 1 steps>0 to SCROLL_RIGHT and the wire agrees - and that asymmetry is the part that would be got wrong by 'just invert it'; two assertions exist to stop it and the negate-both injection proves they do. THE LESSON IS ABOUT EVIDENCE QUALITY. Review re-fetched every source instead of trusting my quotes and corrected the weakest link: my comment credited wl_pointer's spec for 'positive is down', and wayland.xml states no direction at all - the rule is in libinput's header. My conclusion was right and my citation was wrong, which is the kind of error that survives review by anyone who does not go and look. Review also found what I had missed: the SMOOTH portal call has NO portable sign, because KDE negates y and mutter does not, so an obvious future 'upgrade to smooth scrolling for finer granularity' would ship GNOME-correct and KDE-backwards with every test green. Recorded in the code. Also noted on RemEx-whxz that the EIS path carries both this bug and the 120x magnitude one, with nothing to fix until that scaffold is implemented. verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2211/2212.

Implemented Connor's recorded decision: a Known PCs row is inherited across a certificate change ONLY when the re-pair followed confirmCertRepair, because accepting that dialog is the user asserting it is the same machine and nothing else can know it. Old identity captured before forgetHost destroys the pin it derives from; only the nickname is carried, since address/port/timestamp are written by the same connection and an older 'last connected' would sort the PC being used below one untouched for a week. THE LESSON IS WHERE MY TESTS WERE POINTED. I put the decision in a pure function and tested it thoroughly - five tests, three mutations biting - and both defects review found were in the impure half those tests cannot reach. The first made the feature a silent no-op: I cleared the pending repair on ANY successful connection and only then asked whether to migrate, so connecting to a second PC before finishing the re-pair threw the token away. The pure predicate declined correctly and the thing it declined on was already gone - a correct decision made about nothing. Consuming turned out to be its own question and now has its own pure function and tests. The second was a silent relabel of an unrelated PC via plain DHCP address reuse. Extracting logic into a pure core does not make the wiring around it tested; it can make it feel tested. Three doc corrections too, including a comment of mine claiming an ordering guarantee the code does not have and one crediting the wrong mechanism for the old row disappearing - the latter could have led someone to weaken forgetHost's alias union and reintroduce RemEx-1phe. verify.ps1 -Scope android PASS 622/622, was 615.

Covered FilePushOriginator - six tests, about a second, only affordable because the previous iteration made OfferTimeout a seam. THE LESSON IS THAT MY HEADLINE TEST WAS INERT TWICE AND A GREEN RUN SHOWED NOTHING BOTH TIMES. Version one fed a foreign pushId to a single pending offer and asserted the refusal; that passes whether or not Complete routes by id, because FilePushNegotiation.Interpret re-checks the id and refuses the mismatch itself - so the test was re-testing Interpret, which already had seventeen tests, while its comment claimed it tested routing. Mutation caught it. Version two used two concurrent offers so a mis-routed answer would reach the wrong one; also green under the same mutation, because a broken Complete picks an arbitrary ConcurrentDictionary entry and lands on the right one often enough to pass by luck - a discriminator that depends on hash order is not one. What finally worked was TIMING rather than outcome: correct and broken code both end in a refusal, and only correct code leaves the offer still WAITING after a foreign answer arrives. THE GENERALISABLE FORM, recorded on the parent bead for whoever writes the remaining assertions: when a second layer re-checks the same thing your test aims at, no assertion about the OUTCOME can distinguish the layers - find a property only the layer you mean can produce. verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2218/2219.

Pinned that PushFileAsync looks up the /ws/files channel only AFTER the ready handshake - an ordering the code documented and nothing asserted. Observable only because RemEx-gfx3n made ReadyTimeout a seam. THE ASSERTION IS AN ABSENCE, which is normally a weak shape and is safe here only because of the test beside it: AMissingFileChannelSaysWhatWasLookedUpAndWhatIsThere already proves that warning DOES appear when the lookup happens and misses, so a renamed log message breaks that test rather than silently satisfying this one. Without the pair, a DoesNotContain on a log string asserts only that a sentence nobody writes any more is not written. Verified by injection: moving the lookup above the ready wait fails it. Fixed the keep-both livelock on a case-blind mount at the CALL layer, after a previous session had tried the name-search layer and correctly reverted it for breaking a mutation-proven ext4 test. The fix waits for the mount to contradict the listing - proof, not inference - and only then re-resolves case-insensitively; ext4 and Windows are untouched. THREE CORRECTIONS TO GET TERMINATION RIGHT, AND ONLY THE FIRST WAS MINE TO SEE. Review found my convergence claim was broader than the code earned: the relaxed pass only skips a candidate when the LISTING folds onto it under OrdinalIgnoreCase, and a case-blind mount need not fold as .NET does - exFAT maps dotless i onto I where ToUpperInvariant does not, so both passes return the same name and the livelock returns one step later. Review also found the relaxed pass can exhaust the suffix range and return a plan carrying the caller's own overwrite flag, so keep_both plus legacy overwrite:true would have DESTROYED the file the user asked to keep - a data-loss direction the pre-change code did not have. Then my own updated test caught a third: pass two's answer was never checked, so a mount rejecting it too just moved the loop along one name. All three now end in a plain refusal with overwrite off, which gives the user Replace and Skip - outcomes that terminate. THE PATTERN WORTH KEEPING: I reached for 'it converges' as the property and it was really 'it terminates'. Convergence needed a guarantee about the mount's fold table that nothing here can have; termination needed only that I stop when the retry changes nothing. When a guarantee depends on something outside the system, look for the weaker property that does not. Also fixed doc drift review caught - Occupied's remarks still described this livelock as live while citing this bead, which is exactly what sent the previous attempt to the wrong layer. verify.ps1 -Scope dotnet PASS 2227/2228.

Fixed the six LocalContextGetResourceValueCall findings by hoisting the reads into composable scope. A resource read through LocalContext.current is not configuration-aware and can return a stale string after a Configuration change, which matters more here than in most apps because RemEx ships nine locales - a language switch IS that Configuration change. All six sat inside lambdas where stringResource cannot be called because it is @Composable, which is why they were written with a context at all; the fix is a hoist, not a substitution. One takes an argument and only its FORMAT string is hoisted, since the host name is not known until the callback runs - read the template where the locale is live, substitute late. Verified against the tool rather than by inspection: LocalContextGetResourceValueCall 6 -> 0 and the total error count 268 -> 262, exactly six with nothing else moved. Also checked the ten remaining context.getString calls in PairingScreen that lint does NOT flag - they are in helpers taking a context rather than in composables, so there is no composition to read from and nothing to hoist; worth confirming rather than assuming, since a blanket sweep would have 'fixed' them into breakage. With RemEx-28wng earlier, every one of the seven genuine findings from the 269 is now closed, and what remains on RemEx-cljx is purely the suppression decision, which I left for Connor because a suppression is a claim that a rule is wrong for this codebase and that claim should be his.

Split RemEx-9wyu and took its defect half. The remote-desktop idle screen gated its only button on the capability flag alone, and several failure paths also CLEAR that flag - so a failed stream showed its error with nothing to press, and the one thing a user would naturally try was the one thing not offered. THE GATE WAS INCOMPLETE RATHER THAN WRONG, which is why the fix is an OR and not a deletion: hiding the action on a host that genuinely cannot stream is correct, and offering a button that can only fail would be its own defect. An error is simply a different state from an unsupported host, since the flag can be false as a consequence of the failure. Extracted the decision as shouldOfferStartAction rather than widening the condition in place, because the interesting part is the truth table and the case that must not regress - unsupported host, no error, still hidden - is invisible inside a composable. Both directions mutation-verified: reverting to the flag alone restores the dead end, dropping the flag offers a button that can only fail. Third instance this session of the same shape: a mechanism complete except for the step that uses it. The client stamps a ping, the HOST echoes it back with a comment saying it is echoing for a consumer, and RemexNativeClient.HandleMessage had no Pong case at all - so the round trip the timestamp exists for was never computed. Added the case plus a RoundTripTracker. THE GUARD THE BEAD DID NOT MENTION IS THE INTERESTING PART: the ping stamps DateTime.UtcNow, wall clock, and both ends of the subtraction are on the same machine - so an NTP correction between send and receive corrupts exactly one sample and can make it negative. Refusing costs one ping; averaging it in moves the figure for every later sample. Refusals are counted rather than logged because the signal worth having is a RATE of them. Zero ms is accepted rather than refused, since loopback with a coarse clock genuinely produces it and refusing would blank the figure where the connection is best. Deliberately did NOT add the Kotlin callback - the bead warns it must be wired fully through AndroidNativeExports and RemexCoreClient 'or it silently drops', which is exactly the failure I cannot verify here: it would compile, pass everything, and deliver nothing.
